# Decisions: commit-attribution

- 2026-08-13T08:01:32.455Z — rule: **Never record push, merge, or PR state as an event — derive it from git at read time. A commit's initiative never changes, so the recorded half can never go stale; push state changes constantly (force-push, rebase, branch deletion), so recording it would strand a false fact in an append-only log the moment anyone rewrites history.** over Recording push/merge/PR state as events alongside the attribution — the obvious symmetric design, and the one that silently rots. Duplicating the first into the second is how a record starts lying. The whole point of this initiative is a staleness signal a session can trust — a signal built on recorded push state would itself be the next thing to go stale.

Separately, closing the range at session end is an off-by-one that would eat the most important commit of every session, since CLAUDE.md mandates write-back BEFORE the final commit.

- 2026-08-13T08:22:53.671Z — rule: **Never run a git subprocess unconditionally on the hot hook path, and never walk full history — bound every walk, and gate it on a ref actually having moved.** — chose **2.2: the trailer read is a BOUNDED `git log` subprocess that never runs unconditionally on the hot hook path. The hot path keeps doing what readGitState already does — read refs from FILES, no subprocess — and that ref identity is the cache key. The walk is paid only when a ref actually moved (a commit or a push), or on demand from a CLI command. Every walk is bounded (`origin/<branch>..HEAD`, or `-n <k>`), never a full-history walk.** over Putting a `git log` walk directly on the PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit path the way record-integrity 4.4 put push state there; doing a full-history walk and accepting the cost; and parsing commit objects in-process to avoid the subprocess entirely. because Measured on this repo (454 commits, 20 iterations, median): `git rev-parse HEAD` — a trivial command doing no work — costs 8.35ms, which is essentially pure process spawn. A bounded 20-commit trailer walk is 10.35ms, last-100 is 15.55ms, and the full walk is 21.21ms with a 45.25ms tail. The shim budget is 100ms and record-integrity D13 measured 63-67ms already spent, leaving ~33ms — so the full walk's tail alone would blow it, and even the cheapest possible git subprocess eats a quarter of the headroom before doing anything useful. That is precisely why core/git.ts is subprocess-free, and the rule holds. The saving grace is that the expensive answer only changes when a ref moves, and detecting THAT is free by the existing file-based ref read: cheap check on the hot path, expensive walk only on actual change, which is rare. Bounding every walk is what makes it scale — spawn cost is fixed, but a full walk is O(history) and would grow without limit on a large repo, while `origin..HEAD` and `-n k` stay flat. In-process object parsing was rejected: loose objects are inflatable but packed history is not, so it would solve the small case and fail the real one.

A file we did not write is left byte-identical and reported as skipped; our own older one is kept current; `core.hooksPath` is detected first and reported as a skip, because setting it makes `.git/hooks` inert and installing there would look like success while doing nothing. `sofar uninit` mirrors it exactly: it deletes the hook only when our marker is present, never a hand-written one.** over A committed hooks directory wired via core.hooksPath (shared across clones, so attribution would survive a fresh clone); and treating the git hook like the .claude shims, which are sofar-owned and overwritten to stay current. because core.hooksPath is repo-global and would DISABLE every hook already in .git/hooks — buying clone-survival by silently breaking a user's existing tooling is not a trade sofar gets to make on their behalf. And .git/hooks is not version-controlled, so unlike a .claude shim an overwrite there is unrecoverable; that puts it under the .gitattributes law (never clobber, report instead) rather than the shim law. The cost is accepted and real: a fresh clone has NO attribution until someone runs `sofar init`, which is exactly the exposure 2.4's doctor check has to surface. Proven end to end against the local build before being recorded: init installed an executable hook, a commit with no hand-typed trailer came out carrying `Sofar-Initiative: demo-initiative`, two successive amends left exactly one trailer, and a commit made with no session in the environment stayed unattributed rather than guessed.
- 2026-08-13T09:01:06.066Z — rule: **Shipping state is derived locally from git refs only — never by querying GitHub or any forge API.** — chose **3.3: PR state is OUT of scope. Shipping is answered locally and only locally — trailer attribution plus `git rev-list` against the fetched remote ref. sofar makes no network call to GitHub or any forge for this.** over Shelling to `gh pr list` / the GitHub API to report whether an initiative's commits sit in an open or merged PR — which the user explicitly named as part of the original problem ("when push or PR happen…"). because Not on egress grounds, and it matters that a future session knows why: SPEC §Architectural invariants carves out egress that carries no USER CONTENT (the `npm view sofar.sh version` precedent at docs/SPEC.md line 1809), and asking GitHub about a repo GitHub already hosts sends it nothing it does not have. It fails on three other counts instead. First, cost and reliability: a forge round trip is hundreds of milliseconds, varies wildly, and fails offline — it could never sit on the SessionStart path where 3.2's signal lives, so it would have to be a separate on-demand command, a different surface for a strictly weaker fact. Second, it needs `gh` installed and authenticated, a hard external dependency for a marginal increment. Third and decisive: the increment IS marginal. "Merged" is already answered locally by rev-list against the remote ref, so the only genuinely new state is "an open PR exists carrying your work" — the case where the work has NOT landed, which is the least urgent thing a session needs told. Note it would also not rescue the squash-merge gap (2.3), whose fix is reading the commit body. Revisit only if merged-ness stops being answerable locally, e.g. a workflow where initiative work never reaches the local remote ref at all.
- 2026-08-13T09:04:44.992Z — rule: **A review covers watermark..HEAD filtered to this initiative's attributed commits — never a range derived from task or phase timestamps.** — chose **4.1: reviews fire at PHASE BOUNDARIES, and only for initiatives with 3 or more phases. The range for each review is a WATERMARK: the review event records the sha it reviewed through, and the next review covers watermark..HEAD filtered to this initiative's trailer-attributed commits. Ruled by the user 2026-08-13.** over A single review at close (one session instead of N, but it audits every task at maximum surface with the coldest memory, which is where a review is least reliable); phase reviews PLUS a full re-audit at close (N+1 sessions, and the close pass largely re-treads ground — a rubber stamp is worse than no review); reviewing every initiative regardless of size; and opt-in per initiative. because A phase is 3-5 tasks, which fits one session with warm memory and a small diff, so findings arrive while they are still cheap to fix. The cost is real and accepted: one session per phase, so drift-certification would pay 6. The 3-phase floor exists because a 1-phase initiative reviewed by ceremony is how the whole mechanism gets ignored, and an ignored gate is worse than no gate. Opt-in was rejected on the sharper argument: the initiative that drifts is the one where nobody predicted it would, so the flag would be absent precisely when it mattered. The watermark falls out of choosing phase boundaries and is what makes the range tractable — phases have no commit boundaries of their own, and deriving them from task timestamps would be the time-window guess record-integrity D6 already rejected.

It is scoped to the four questions a per-phase review structurally cannot answer — goal conformance (does the finished thing achieve the initiative's stated goal), cross-phase drift (did a later phase violate a decision taken in an earlier one), integration (each phase passed alone; do they compose), and unresolved findings carried forward. It must NOT re-audit per-phase correctness. Not through a peer message. Raised by the user 2026-08-13.** over Sending a SendMessage peer notification when a session pushes; and leaving the signal at SessionStart only, where 3.2 put it. because 3.2's notice fires once per session, so a session already RUNNING when a sibling pushes learns nothing until it restarts — which is the user's original complaint still open in exactly the case they described. Peer messaging was rejected on two grounds: the pushing session would have to know which peers to tell and which initiatives their commits belonged to, reintroducing coordination the derived design removed; and a message is transport, never storage, so the fact would live in a chat rather than in the record that already holds it. The ref-gate is what D6 anticipated when it forbade unconditional subprocesses on the hot path — it is not an exception to that rule, it is the escape the rule was written with. It also stays honest under concurrency: refs are shared across sessions in one worktree, so a peer's push updates them for everyone at once with nothing to broadcast.

Raised by the user 2026-08-13.** over D3's original wording, which had the packet NAME `/code-review` and `/simplify` outright as the instruction — shipped in 4.2 and 4.3 and wrong the moment sofar runs anywhere but Claude Code. because sofar is host-agnostic by construction — `sofar init` writes an AGENTS.md convention dialect specifically for tools with no MCP (BD31), and the CLI surface exists so the whole loop works without Claude Code at all. Auto-writing DECISIONS was rejected firmly: a decision here carries chose/over/because and is something a person or agent RULED, and manufacturing them from statistics would put inferred claims in the one log whose trustworthiness this codebase runs a whole certification initiative to defend. A wrong inferred decision would then render verbatim in every digest forever. Suggest-and-confirm keeps the inference out of the record until something ratifies it. Scope limit worth stating plainly: only Bash commands are observable, because the PostToolUse matcher is Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash and every other tool name appends nothing — so a CLI linter is learnable today and a slash-command skill is not, and closing that needs a hook-surface change judged on its own merits.
